questions.problem:
Consider the following boundary value problem (BVP).

$$
{y}^{″}-4{y}^{′}+3y=2x,\,y(0)=3,\,y(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1
$$

Let ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ be fundamental solutions of the form $y={e}^{mx}$ to the corresponding homogeneous differential equation, and suppose we define the matrix $A$ as 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(0) & {y}_{2}(0) \\ {y}_{1}(1) & {y}_{2}(1)\end{aligned}].
$$

Fill in the correct options in the reasoning below **without calculating the solution** to this BVP.

$\,$ The **absolute value** of $det(A)$ is {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the corresponding homogeneous BVP {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, our inhomogeneous BVP {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the second-order inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP)

$$
{y}^{″}(x)+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=f(x),\,a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)={\gamma }_{1},\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)={\gamma }_{2}
$$

where $P,Q,$ and $f$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i}$ and ${\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ 

The inhomogeneous BVP has at most one solution if and only if the associated homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Specifically:

- If the homogeneous BVP has the unique solution $y≡0,$ then the inhomogeneous problem has a unique solution.

- If the homogeneous BVP has (infinitely many) nontrivial solutions, then the inhomogeneous problem either has infinitely many solutions or no solution.

Let ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ be a fundamental set of solutions to the corresponding homogeneous differential equation ${y}^{″}+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0.$ 

To classify the solutions of the corresponding homogeneous BVP, we define the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}\,{\alpha }_{1}{y}_{1}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}(a) & {\alpha }_{1}{y}_{2}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}(a) \\ {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{1}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}(b) & {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{2}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}(b)\end{aligned}].
$$

The homogeneous BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y≡0$ if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$ In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the homogeneous BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Dirichlet boundary conditions. So, setting ${\alpha }_{i}=1,{\beta }_{i}=0,a=0,$ and $b=1,$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(0) & {y}_{2}(0) \\ {y}_{1}(1) & {y}_{2}(1)\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-4m+3 & =0 \\ (m-1)(m-3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=1$ and $m=3,$ and so the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x},\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{3x}.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ e & {e}^{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|det(A)| & =|1\cdot {e}^{3}-1\cdot e| \\  & =|{e}^{3}-e| \\  & =e({e}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(A)\ne 0,$ the corresponding homogeneous BVP $\text{has the unique solution }y≡0.$

Therefore, since the corresponding homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution $y≡0$, our inhomogeneous BVP $\text{has a unique solution}.$

choices.value: has infinitely many solutions or no solution

$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)={\gamma }_{1},\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)={\gamma }_{2}
$$

where $P,Q,$ and $f$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i}$ and ${\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ 

The inhomogeneous BVP has at most one solution if and only if the associated homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Specifically:

- If the homogeneous BVP has the unique solution $y≡0,$ then the inhomogeneous problem either has no solution or a unique solution.

- If the homogeneous BVP has (infinitely many) nontrivial solutions, then the inhomogeneous problem either has infinitely many solutions or no solution.

To classify the solutions of the corresponding homogeneous BVP, we define the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}\,{\alpha }_{1}{y}_{1}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}(a) & {\alpha }_{1}{y}_{2}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}(a) \\ {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{1}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}(b) & {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{2}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}(b)\end{aligned}].
$$

The homogeneous BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y≡0$ if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$ In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the homogeneous BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Neumann boundary conditions. So, setting ${\alpha }_{i}=0,{\beta }_{i}=1,a=0,$ and $b=\pi ,$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{′}(0) & {y}_{2}^{′}(0) \\ {y}_{1}^{′}(\pi ) & {y}_{2}^{′}(\pi )\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+49 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 7\text{i}.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡7x,\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡7x.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
{y}_{1}^{′}(x)=-7\operatorname{sin}⁡7x,\,{y}_{2}^{′}(x)=7\operatorname{cos}⁡7x.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-7\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\cdot 0) & 7\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\cdot 0) \\ -7\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\cdot \pi ) & 7\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\cdot \pi )\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 7 \\ 0 & -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|det(A)| & =|0\cdot (-7)-7\cdot 0| \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(A)=0,$ the corresponding homogeneous BVP $\text{has infinitely many solutions}.$

Therefore, since the corresponding homogeneous BVP has (infinitely many) nontrivial solutions, our inhomogeneous BVP $\text{has infinitely many solutions or no solution}.$

questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the second-order inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP)

$$
{y}^{″}(x)+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=f(x),\,a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)={\gamma }_{1},\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)={\gamma }_{2}
$$

where $P,Q,$ and $f$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i}$ and ${\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ 

If the associated homogeneous BVP has nontrivial solutions, then the inhomogeneous BVP has either no solution or infinitely many solutions. 

To find the solution of an inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP):

- First, we find the general solution ${y}_{h}(x)$ of the corresponding homogeneous equation.

- Then, we find a particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ of the inhomogeneous equation.

- Finally, we apply the boundary conditions to determine the arbitrary constants.

However, in this particular case, we can integrate the equation directly. By doing so, we get the general solution

$$
y=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+Ax+B.
$$

 

Note that the derivative ${y}^{′}$ is

$$
{y}^{′}={x}^{2}+A.
$$

Applying the condition $y(0)=0$ gives

$$
B=0.
$$

So, we have 

$$
y=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+Ax.
$$

 

Applying the condition $y(1)-{y}^{′}(1)=-\frac{2}{3}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(\frac{1}{3}+A)-(1+A) & =-\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}+A-1-A & =-\frac{2}{3} \\ A-A & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

which is automatically satisfied for any $A.$

Therefore, the solution to the boundary value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+Ax.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
f(x)=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3},\,g(x)=x.
$$

**Note**: The associated homogeneous BVP

$$
{y}^{″}=0,\,y(0)=0,\,y(1)-{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1
$$

has infinitely many solutions. Therefore, the inhomogeneous BVP has either infinitely many solutions or no solution. Since we have found a solution that contains an arbitrary constant and satisfies both boundary conditions, the BVP has infinitely many solutions.

Suppose we have the second-order inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP)

$$
{y}^{″}(x)+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=f(x),\,a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)={\gamma }_{1},\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)={\gamma }_{2}
$$

where $P,Q,$ and $f$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i}$ and ${\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ 

The inhomogeneous BVP has at most one solution if and only if the associated homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution $y≡0.$ 

To find the solution of an inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP):

- First, we find the general solution ${y}_{h}(x)$ of the corresponding homogeneous equation.

- Then, we find a particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ of the inhomogeneous equation.

- Finally, we apply the boundary conditions to determine the arbitrary constants.

The homogeneous equation is

$$
{y}^{″}-2{y}^{′}+y=0.
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-2m+1 & =0 \\ (m-1)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a repeated root $m=1.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{x}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the homogeneous equation is

$$
{y}_{h}=(A+Bx){e}^{x}.
$$

Now, we seek a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=D.
$$

Substituting this into our inhomogeneous equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(D)^{″}-2(D)^{′}+(D) & =4 \\ D & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}=4
$$

and the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={y}_{h}+{y}_{p} \\  & =(A+Bx){e}^{x}+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(A+B(x+1)){e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the condition ${y}^{′}(-1)=0$ gives

$$
A{e}^{-1}=0\,⇒\,A=0.
$$

So, we have 

$$
{y}^{′}=B(x+1){e}^{x}.
$$

Applying the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=1$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}B(0+1){e}^{0} & =1\,⇒\,B=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for the function $g(x),$ we have

$$
g(x)={y}_{p}(x)=4.
$$

**Note**: The associated homogeneous BVP

$$
{y}^{″}-2{y}^{′}+y=0,\,{y}^{′}(-1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,-1\le x\le 0
$$

has only the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Therefore, the inhomogeneous BVP has at most one solution. Since we have found a solution satisfying both boundary conditions, the solution to this inhomogeneous BVP is unique.

questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the second-order inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP)

$$
{y}^{″}(x)+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=f(x),\,a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)={\gamma }_{1},\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)={\gamma }_{2}
$$

where $P,Q,$ and $f$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i}$ and ${\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ 

The inhomogeneous BVP has at most one solution if and only if the associated homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution $y≡0.$ 

To find the solution of an inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP):

- First, we find the general solution ${y}_{h}(x)$ of the corresponding homogeneous equation.

- Then, we find a particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ of the inhomogeneous equation.

- Finally, we apply the boundary conditions to determine the arbitrary constants.

The homogeneous equation is

$$
{y}^{″}-{y}^{′}-2y=0.
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-m-2 & =0 \\ (m-2)(m+1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=2$ and $m=-1.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{2x},\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-x}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the homogeneous equation is

$$
{y}_{h}=A{e}^{2x}+B{e}^{-x}.
$$

Now, we seek a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=D.
$$

Substituting this into our inhomogeneous equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(D)^{″}-(D)^{′}-2(D) & =6 \\ -2D & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $D,$ we get

$$
D=-3.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}=-3
$$

and the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={y}_{h}+{y}_{p} \\  & =A{e}^{2x}+B{e}^{-x}-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2A{e}^{2x}-B{e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the condition ${y}^{′}(3)={e}^{6}$ gives

$$
2A{e}^{6}-B{e}^{-3}={e}^{6}\,⇒\,A=\frac{1}{2}(B{e}^{-9}+1).
$$

So, we have 

$$
{y}^{′}=(B{e}^{-9}+1){e}^{2x}-B{e}^{-x},
$$

 

Applying the condition ${y}^{′}(4)={e}^{8}$ gives

$$
(B{e}^{-9}+1){e}^{8}-B{e}^{-4}={e}^{8}\,⇒\,B=0.
$$

Substituting back into the first equation and solving for $A,$ we have

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}(B{e}^{-9}+1)=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, for the function $g(x),$ we have

$$
g(x)={y}_{p}(x)=-3.
$$

**Note**: The associated homogeneous BVP

$$
{y}^{″}-{y}^{′}-2y=0,\,{y}^{′}(3)=0,\,{y}^{′}(4)=0,\,3\le x\le 4
$$

has only the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Therefore, the inhomogeneous BVP has at most one solution. Since we have found a solution satisfying both boundary conditions, the solution to this inhomogeneous BVP is unique.

Suppose we have the second-order inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP)

$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
\alpha_1 y(a) + \beta_1 y'(a) = \gamma_1, \qquad

$$

where $P, Q,$ and $f$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and $\alpha_i$ and $\beta_i$ are real constants such that $(\alpha_i, \beta_i) \neq (0,0).$ 

The inhomogeneous BVP has at most one solution if and only if the associated homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution $y \equiv 0.$ Specifically:

- If the homogeneous BVP has the unique solution $y \equiv 0,$ then the inhomogeneous problem either has no solution or a unique solution.

- If the homogeneous BVP has (infinitely many) nontrivial solutions, then the inhomogeneous problem either has infinitely many solutions or no solution.

To classify the solutions of the corresponding homogeneous BVP, we define the matrix $A$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+16 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m = \pm 4\textrm i.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
y_1(x) = \cos 4x, \qquad y_2(x) = \sin 4x.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
y_1'(x) = -4\sin 4x, \qquad y_2'(x) = 4\cos 4x.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot 0) & 4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot 0) \\ -4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \pi ) & 4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \pi )\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

y''(x) + P(x)y' + Q(x)y = f(x), \qquad a \leq x \leq b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
\alpha_1 y(a) + \beta_1 y'(a) = \gamma_1, \qquad 
\alpha_2 y(b) + \beta_2 y'(b) = \gamma_2
$$

where $P, Q,$ and $f$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and $\alpha_i$ and $\beta_i$ are real constants such that $(\alpha_i, \beta_i) \neq (0,0).$ 

If the associated homogeneous BVP has nontrivial solutions, then the inhomogeneous BVP has either no solution or infinitely many solutions. 

To find the solution of an inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP):

- First, we find the general solution $y_h(x)$ of the corresponding homogeneous equation.

- Then, we find a particular solution $y_p(x)$ of the inhomogeneous equation.

- Finally, we apply the boundary conditions to determine the arbitrary constants.

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y = e^{m x}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+16 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m = \pm 4\textrm i.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
y_1(x) = \cos 4x, \qquad y_2(x) = \sin 4x
$$

and the general solution to the homogeneous equation is

$$
y_h = A\cos 4x + B\sin 4x.
$$

Next, we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
y_p(x) = Cx\cos 4x + Dx\sin 4x
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′}(x) & =C\operatorname{cos}⁡4x-4Cx\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+D\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+4Dx\operatorname{cos}⁡4x \\ {y}_{p}^{″}(x) & =-8C\operatorname{sin}⁡4x-16Cx\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+8D\operatorname{cos}⁡4x-16Dx\operatorname{sin}⁡4x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation, we reach (after some cancellation)

$$
\begin{aligned}-8C\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+8D\operatorname{cos}⁡4x=\operatorname{sin}⁡4x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives $C = -\dfrac18$ and $D = 0.$ Therefore, our general solution is

$$
y = A\cos 4x + B\sin 4x -\dfrac18x\cos4x.
$$

Applying the condition $y(0) = 0$ gives

$$
A\cos (4\cdot 0) + B\sin (4\cdot 0) - \dfrac18 \cdot 0 \cdot \cos (4\cdot 0) = 0
$$

which gives $A = 0.$ So, we have

$$
y = B\sin 4x -\dfrac18x\cos 4x.
$$

Applying the condition $y(\pi) = -\dfrac\pi8$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\pi )-\frac{\pi }{8}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\pi )=-\frac{\pi }{8} \\ 0-\frac{\pi }{8}=-\frac{\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

which is true for all values of $B$

Therefore, the solution to the boundary value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =-\frac{1}{8}x\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+B\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡4x.\end{aligned}
$$

where $B$ is arbitrary.

Finally, 

$$
f(x) = -\dfrac18 x\cos 4x, \qquad g(x) = \sin 4x.
$$

**Note**: The associated homogeneous BVP

$$
y''  + 16y = 0,  \qquad y(0) = 0, \quad y(\pi) = 0,\quad 0\leq x \leq \pi
$$

has infinitely many solutions. Therefore, the inhomogeneous BVP has either infinitely many solutions or no solution. Since we have found a solution that contains an arbitrary constant and satisfies both boundary conditions, the BVP has infinitely many solutions.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving Solvable Inhomogeneous BVPs With a Unique Solutions
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following boundary value problem (BVP).

$$
y'' - 9y = -9x - 3,  \qquad y(1) =  \dfrac{4}{3}, \quad y(2) = \dfrac{13}{3},\quad 1\leq x \leq 2
$$

The solution is given by

$$
y = Ae^{3x} + Be^{-3x} + g(x).
$$

Find the constants $A$ and $B,$ and the function $g(x).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the second-order inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP)

$$
y''(x) + P(x)y' + Q(x)y = f(x), \qquad a \leq x \leq b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
\alpha_1 y(a) + \beta_1 y'(a) = \gamma_1, \qquad 
\alpha_2 y(b) + \beta_2 y'(b) = \gamma_2
$$

where $P, Q,$ and $f$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and $\alpha_i$ and $\beta_i$ are real constants such that $(\alpha_i, \beta_i) \neq (0,0).$ 

The inhomogeneous BVP has at most one solution if and only if the associated homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution $y \equiv 0.$ 

To find the solution of an inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP):

- First, we find the general solution $y_h(x)$ of the corresponding homogeneous equation.

- Then, we find a particular solution $y_p(x)$ of the inhomogeneous equation.

- Finally, we apply the boundary conditions to determine the arbitrary constants.

The homogeneous equation is

$$
y'' - 9y  = 0.
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y = e^{m x}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-9 & =0 \\ (m-3)(m+3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m = 3$ and $m = -3.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
y_1(x) = e^{3x}, \qquad y_2(x) = e^{-3x}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the homogeneous equation is

$$
y_h = Ae^{3x} + Be^{-3x}.
$$

Now, we seek a particular solution $y_p$ of the form

$$
y_p = Cx + D.
$$

Substituting this into our inhomogeneous equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(Cx+D)^{″}-9(Cx+D) & =-9x-3 \\ -9(Cx+D) & =-9x-3 \\ -9Cx-9D & =-9x-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients of $x$ and constants, respectively, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-9C=-9\, & ⇒\,C=1 \\ -9D=-3\, & ⇒\,D=\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
y_p = x + \dfrac13
$$

and the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={y}_{h}+{y}_{p} \\  & =A{e}^{3x}+B{e}^{-3x}+x+\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the condition $y(1) =  \dfrac{4}{3}$ gives

$$
Ae^3 + Be^{-3} +\dfrac43 =  \dfrac{4}{3} \qquad \Rightarrow\qquad B = - Ae^6.
$$

So, we have 

$$
y = Ae^{3x} - Ae^{-3x+6} + x +\dfrac13.
$$

 

Applying the condition $y(2) = \dfrac{13}{3}$ gives

$$
Ae^6 - Ae^{0} +2 + \dfrac13 = \dfrac{13}{3} \qquad \Rightarrow\qquad Ae^6 - A  = 2.
$$

Solving for $A,$ we have

$$
A = \dfrac{2}{e^6-1}.
$$

Substituting back into the first equation and solving for $B,$ we have

$$
B = - Ae^6 = -\dfrac{2e^6}{e^6-1}.
$$

Finally, for the function $g(x),$ we have

$$
g(x) = y_p(x) = x + \dfrac13.
$$

**Note**: The associated homogeneous BVP

$$
y'' - 9y = 0,  \qquad y(1) = 0, \quad y(2) = 0,\quad 1\leq x \leq 2
$$

has only the trivial solution $y\equiv 0.$ Therefore, the inhomogeneous BVP has at most one solution. Since we have found a solution satisfying both boundary conditions, the solution to this inhomogeneous BVP is unique.
